title: Leveraging Latent Visual Reasoning in Silence
claim: Replacing or removing an intermediate special component barely changes performance, so its value lies in shaping learning rather than inference-time use.
layout: Top row of three token-sequence variants, below two bar-chart panels, shared legend at bottom
description: The top strip shows a cat-counting question in a grey rounded box. To its right are three token-sequence rows, each ending in the answer 'Two.' Row 1 uses real latent tokens (green squares between S and E markers). Row 2 replaces them with orange question-mark random tokens. Row 3 removes them, shown as a dashed empty slot. A bracket on the right points to a cream box reading 'All correct, Latents not utilized'. Below are two grouped bar charts, LVR-SFT and Monet-SFT. They report accuracy on V*, MMVP and MathVista, with green, orange and grey bars that are nearly equal in height. Red dotted lines marked 'Ours' sit above the bars. A legend at the bottom explains the token types and symbols.
caption: When standard latent tokens (green) are replaced with random values (yellow) or completely removed (grey), latent visual reasoning models retain comparable or achieve even higher performance across benchmarks. We demonstrate that latent reasoning may have limited value as a mandatory inference-time format, but can still be leveraged in silence to improve learning (red).
abstract: Latent visual reasoning involves visual evidence more directly in multimodal reasoning by inserting continuous latent tokens before textual generation. However, the necessity of these latent tokens at inference remains ambiguous. We show that replacing latent tokens with random noise or removing them completely causes little performance degradation across spatial reasoning benchmarks. Reinforcement learning further diminishes the latent generation behavior after post-training. These observations raise a central question: \textit{Is latent visual reasoning still meaningful}? We argue that its value should be measured by how effectively latent tokens guide learning, rather than whether they persist as an inference-time format. Our analysis shows that latent reasoning is unevenly favorable across question types, yet hard task-level routing for applying latent generation is brittle. Motivated by these findings, we propose an attention-based reward that encourages generated latent tokens to interact with later text tokens during RL. This reward promotes latent utilization when the latent mode is activated while preserving the flexibility to use pure-text reasoning. Experiments show that our method improves performance across perception and visual reasoning benchmarks, even when latent tokens are rarely generated after post-training. Our results highlight that, without explicit expression at inference, latent visual reasoning can shape better visual grounding and more accurate textual reasoning \textbf{in silence}.
